thought_title: God's hidden plan to save through the Son
orientation: The author is explaining how God, having already arranged everything with his Son, first let humanity be carried away by sin and then revealed his kindness by giving the Son as a ransom.
pass_a_gloss: Having therefore already arranged all things with the Son in himself, until the former time he let us, as we wished, be carried by disorderly impulses, led away by pleasures and desires. Not at all rejoicing in our sins, but bearing with them, nor approving the then season of unrighteousness, but creating the present season of righteousness, so that, having been convicted in the former time by our own works as unworthy of life, we might now be made worthy by the kindness of God, and, having shown that by ourselves it is impossible to enter into the kingdom of God, we might become able by the power of God. And when our unrighteousness had been filled up and had been completely revealed, because its wages, punishment and death, were expected, and the season came, which God appointed henceforth to reveal his own kindness and power — O the surpassing love for humanity and love of God — he did not hate us nor reject us nor bear a grudge, but he was patient, he bore with us, he himself in mercy took up our sins, he himself gave his own Son as a ransom for us, the holy one for the lawless, the innocent one for the wicked, the righteous one for the unrighteous, the incorruptible one for the corruptible, the immortal one for the mortals. For what else was able to cover our sins except that one's righteousness? In whom is it possible for us, lawless and impious, to be justified except in the Son of God alone? O the sweet exchange, O the unsearchable workmanship, O the unexpected benefits, so that the lawlessness of many might be hidden in one righteous man, and the righteousness of one might justify many lawless people. Having therefore convicted in the former time the inability of our nature to attain life, and now having shown the Savior able to save even the impossible, from both he wished us to trust in his kindness, to regard him as nourisher, father, teacher, counselor, physician, mind, light, honor, glory, strength, life, not to be anxious about clothing and food.

choices.why: Keeps the literal sense of unruly, undisciplined movements carrying us along, matching the passive φέρεσθαι.
Literal sense of enduring or putting up with, distinct from approval; pairs with the later ἠνέσχετο.
Literal sense of fashioning or making; the author uses the verb to show God actively producing the present season of righteousness.
The middle aorist of ἀποδίδωμι means to give up or hand over as a price; 'gave over' preserves the transactional force without importing 'sold'.
Literal sense of a swap or exchange, capturing the rhetorical wonder at the substitution of the righteous one for sinners.
Literal sense of a crafted work or creation, echoing the earlier δημιουργῶν and pointing to God's saving act as a work of craft.

pass_b_english: So when he had already arranged everything in his own mind together with his Son, he let us go on as we wished until the former time, carried along by disorderly impulses, by pleasures and desires. He was not at all rejoicing in our sins, but bearing with them. He was not approving the season of unrighteousness that then existed, but creating the present season of righteousness. His purpose was this: after we were convicted by our own works in that former time as unworthy of life, we might now be made worthy by the kindness of God, and after we had shown that we could not enter the kingdom of God by ourselves, we might become able to do so by the power of God.

But when our unrighteousness had reached its full measure and it had been made completely clear that its wages were expected to be punishment and death, then the time came that God had appointed to reveal at last his own kindness and power. Oh, the surpassing love of God for humanity! He did not hate us, or reject us, or remember our sins against us. Instead he was patient, he bore with us, and in his mercy he took our sins upon himself. He gave over his own Son as a ransom for us: the holy one for the lawless, the innocent one for the wicked, the righteous one for the unrighteous, the incorruptible one for the corruptible, the immortal one for the mortal.

For what else could cover our sins except his righteousness? In whom could we, lawless and impious as we are, be made righteous except in the Son of God alone? Oh, the sweet exchange! Oh, the unsearchable workmanship! Oh, the unexpected benefits! For the lawlessness of many was hidden in one righteous man, and the righteousness of one made many lawless people righteous.

So after he had convicted our nature in the former time of its inability to attain life, and had now shown the Savior able to save even what is impossible, he willed us to trust in his kindness from both of these things, and to regard him as nourisher, father, teacher, counselor, physician, mind, light, honor, glory, strength, and life, and not to worry about clothing and food.

last_rejected.quote: the surpassing love of God for humanity
last_rejected.source_quote: ὢ τῆς ὑπερβαλλούσης φιλανθρωπίας καὶ ἀγάπης τοῦ θεοῦ
last_rejected.why: Source has two distinct nouns: philanthrōpias (love for humanity) AND agapēs (love). English merges them into one.
last_rejected.fix: the surpassing love for humanity and love of God
last_rejected.ruling: English combines φιλανθρωπίας and ἀγάπης into one phrase, but still conveys God’s surpassing love for humanity; nuance loss is minor.

polish.changed: Clarified the purpose clause in the first paragraph, made the subject of each action explicit, and smoothed sentence rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.why: No explanation that this refers to Jesus, the Son of God.
notes.fix: Introduce “the Son (Jesus Christ)” when first mentioned.

variants.text: the Word appeared and spoke with boldness

notes.why: The Son/Christ is called by several different titles across sections; a first-time reader may not realize all refer to the same figure.
notes.fix: Briefly note on first use that 'Word,' 'Son,' 'child,' and 'only-begotten' all refer to Christ.
